title: Thinking recursively
description: Recognize the pattern. Build the solution. Make it faster.

parts.title: Your starting point
parts.label: Pre-test
parts.description: A short, unassisted check of what you already know. This is a baseline, not a lesson grade.
parts.question: Complete the four diagnostic questions without assistance.

parts.title: A smaller version of the same problem
parts.label: Discover
parts.description: Open the nesting dolls, watch the calls build up, then follow the returns back out.
parts.question: Explain base cases, recursive reduction, and pending calls or stack unwinding, using the nesting dolls and worked Fibonacci example.
parts.theory: Recursion solves a problem using smaller instances of the same problem. A base case is handled directly without another recursive call. A recursive case reduces the input and uses the smaller result. Calls wait on a stack until their subproblems return. In the Russian nesting doll analogy, opening a doll reveals a smaller similar doll; the smallest solid doll is the base case. Then results return outward, one waiting call at a time. Use this analogy conversationally and ask one brief check-in question at a time.

parts.title: Choose, build, and trace
parts.label: Build & trace
parts.description: Use the worked Fibonacci example to design a naive Climbing Stairs solution, then construct and trace your own call tree.
parts.question: There are n stairs, with moves of one or two stairs. Explain why recursion suits this problem, write climb_stairs(n), and construct the full naive call tree for n=5. For zero stairs, count the empty sequence as one way.
parts.theory: Climbing Stairs has branching self-similar subproblems: after a move of one or two stairs, count ways to cover the remaining stairs. With the empty sequence counted once, ways(0)=1 and ways(1)=1, and ways(n)=ways(n-1)+ways(n-2) for n>1. The standard naive n=5 tree has 15 calls, returns 8, and reaches five stack frames when the root counts as one. Other valid base-case conventions can expand n=1 into n=0 and n=-1, where negative inputs return zero. Do not reveal these answers or write the learner's function; ask targeted questions about progress, termination, and combining smaller results.

parts.title: Remember the work you have already done
parts.label: Optimize
parts.description: Study a worked Fibonacci cache example, locate redundancy in your own stairs tree, then memoize your own stairs code.
parts.question: Explain the worked Fibonacci cache example. In your own Climbing Stairs tree, count repeated states and redundant calls. Refactor climb_stairs(n) with a dictionary and explain time and memory use.
parts.theory: In naive fib(5), fib(2) occurs three times and fib(3) twice. A worked example shows lookup before recursion and storage before return. The learner applies that pattern to their own Climbing Stairs code and tree. In the standard stairs(5) tree, stairs(2) occurs three times, so two of those computations repeat work. Memoized Climbing Stairs uses O(n) time, O(n) dictionary space, and O(n) stack depth under unit-cost arithmetic and dictionary access. This is top-down dynamic programming. Guide with small hints; do not provide complete code or the full answers.

parts.title: A new problem, on your own
parts.label: Transfer
parts.description: Apply what you learned to Grid Unique Paths, without AI support, hints, or reference answers.
parts.question: Count paths from the top-left to bottom-right of a rows-by-cols grid of cells, moving only right or down, with no obstacles. An empty grid has zero paths; a one-cell grid has one path using no moves. Explain base conditions, reduction, and pending calls before running code. Write unique_paths(rows, cols), construct a naive tree for (3,3), identify overlap, and refactor with a dictionary. Explain runtime and memory in terms of both grid dimensions.

pretest.prompt: Given fib(0)=0, fib(1)=1, and fib(n)=fib(n-1)+fib(n-2), what does fib(4) return?
In the full naive fib(4) call tree, how many times is fib(2) called?
How does the runtime of naive recursive Fibonacci grow as n increases?
Before this lesson, have you implemented recursive memoization using a dictionary?
options: I have seen it or followed an example
Yes, I have implemented it independently
